### Genetic Instruments and Mendelian Randomization {#sec-mendelian-randomization}

Mendelian randomization instruments an exposure with genetic variants. The appeal is an
appealingly literal randomization argument: alleles are assigned at conception by the independent
assortment of chromosomes, before any of the confounders that trouble observational epidemiology
have a chance to operate, so a variant that shifts an exposure is a lottery ticket for that
exposure. @davey2003mendelian set out the framework, and it has since become the dominant design
in epidemiology and has moved into economics through genoeconomics [@vonhinke2016genetic].

It is worth studying even for a reader with no interest in genetics, because the field has
developed the most sophisticated toolkit anywhere for the problem of many weak, possibly invalid
instruments, and that toolkit generalizes.

#### Setup: Two-Sample Summary-Data MR

Modern practice rarely uses individual-level data. Instead it uses published genome-wide
association study coefficients from two different samples: $\hat\gamma_j$, the estimated effect of
variant $j$ on the exposure, and $\hat\Gamma_j$, its estimated effect on the outcome. If variant
$j$ is a valid instrument, the ratio $\hat\Gamma_j / \hat\gamma_j$ estimates the causal effect
$\beta$, and the variants can be combined.

The inverse-variance weighted estimator of @burgess2013mendelian is the workhorse:

$$
\hat\beta_{\text{IVW}} = \frac{\sum_j w_j \hat\gamma_j \hat\Gamma_j}{\sum_j w_j \hat\gamma_j^2},
\qquad w_j = 1/\text{se}(\hat\Gamma_j)^2 .
$$

This is exactly two-stage least squares written in summary statistics, and it is equivalent to a
weighted regression of $\hat\Gamma$ on $\hat\gamma$ through the origin.

The threat is pleiotropy: a variant that affects the outcome through a pathway other than the
exposure violates the exclusion restriction. Two refinements address it. MR-Egger
[@bowden2015mendelian] frees the intercept in that weighted regression; under the assumption that
pleiotropic effects are independent of instrument strength, the slope is consistent and the
intercept is a test for directional pleiotropy. The weighted median estimator
[@bowden2016consistent] is consistent when at least half the weight sits on valid instruments.
MR-PRESSO [@verbanck2018detection] detects and removes outlying variants.

#### Demonstration

The simulation below constructs summary statistics for forty variants at magnitudes typical of a
well-powered study, under three pleiotropy regimes. The true causal effect is 0.3 throughout.

```{r mriv-demo, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(404)

mr_once <- function(J = 40, regime = "none", frac = 0.4, beta = 0.3) {
  gam <- runif(J, 0.05, 0.20)                       # variant -> exposure
  alpha <- switch(regime,
    none        = rep(0, J),
    balanced    = rnorm(J, 0, 0.03),                # mean-zero pleiotropy
    directional = { a <- rep(0, J)
                    a[seq_len(round(frac * J))] <-
                      abs(rnorm(round(frac * J), 0.04, 0.01)); a })
  Gam  <- alpha + beta * gam                        # variant -> outcome
  se_g <- rep(0.01, J); se_G <- rep(0.015, J)
  gh <- gam + rnorm(J, 0, se_g)                     # published estimates
  Gh  <- Gam + rnorm(J, 0, se_G)

  w <- 1 / se_G^2
  ivw <- sum(w * gh * Gh) / sum(w * gh^2)           # inverse-variance weighted
  eg  <- coef(lm(Gh ~ gh, weights = w))             # MR-Egger
  ratio <- Gh / gh; se_r <- se_G / abs(gh)          # weighted median
  o <- order(ratio)
  cw <- cumsum((1 / se_r^2)[o]) / sum(1 / se_r^2)
  c(IVW = ivw, Egger_slope = unname(eg[2]), Egger_intercept = unname(eg[1]),
    Weighted_median = ratio[o][which.min(abs(cw - 0.5))])
}

tab <- t(sapply(c("none", "balanced", "directional"), function(r)
  round(rowMeans(replicate(300, mr_once(regime = r))), 4)))
knitr::kable(tab,
  caption = paste("Summary-data Mendelian randomization estimators under three",
                  "pleiotropy regimes. The true causal effect is 0.300."))
```

Three lessons are visible in the table.

Balanced pleiotropy does not bias the inverse-variance weighted estimator. When the invalid
pathways are mean zero across variants, the violations average out, and the estimator is as
accurate as under no pleiotropy at all. This is the reason the design tolerates a great deal of
biological messiness.

Directional pleiotropy does bias it, and substantially: the estimate rises from 0.30 to roughly
0.41 when forty percent of the variants carry a same-signed invalid pathway. The MR-Egger
intercept moves away from zero, which is what makes it a diagnostic, and the Egger slope stays
close to the truth. The weighted median sits between the two, partially robust because more than
half the weight is still on valid variants.

The fact that the diagnostic exists at all is what makes this literature worth borrowing from.
In a conventional design with one instrument there is nothing to compare, and the exclusion
restriction is simply asserted. With many instruments the heterogeneity of the individual ratio
estimates becomes evidence, and the pattern of that heterogeneity distinguishes balanced from
directional violations.

#### Limits

The design is not the clean lottery the assortment argument suggests.

Population stratification breaks the randomization: if allele frequencies and the outcome both
vary with ancestry, the variant is correlated with confounders through ancestry, which is why
analyses are restricted to genetically homogeneous samples and adjusted for principal components
of the genotype matrix.

Weak instruments are endemic, since individual variants explain a tiny share of exposure
variance. In one-sample MR the bias is toward the observational association, which is the
direction that makes a spurious finding look like a confirmation. Two-sample designs with
non-overlapping samples bias toward zero instead, which is safer but not harmless.

Linkage disequilibrium means variants are correlated with their neighbours, so a variant may
proxy for a nearby gene with an entirely different function. Canalization, the developmental
compensation for a lifelong genetic perturbation, means the estimand is the effect of lifetime
exposure, not the effect of the intervention a policymaker might actually make. That last point is
the sharpest one for applied economics: a genetic variant that raises lifetime body mass index
does not identify the effect of a diet program, and the LATE framework of
Section \@ref(sec-monotonicity-assumption) applies with full force.

#### Practice

1.  Report instrument strength as the $F$ statistic or the share of exposure variance explained,
    and say whether the samples overlap, since the direction of weak-instrument bias depends on it.
2.  Report IVW, MR-Egger, and weighted median together. Agreement across estimators with different
    robustness properties is the substitute for an untestable exclusion restriction.
3.  Report the MR-Egger intercept explicitly as the directional pleiotropy test.
4.  Show a leave-one-out analysis. A result driven by a single variant is a result about that gene.
5.  State the estimand as the effect of lifelong exposure and resist translating it into the effect
    of a policy without a separate argument.
6.  Restrict to a genetically homogeneous sample and adjust for ancestry components, and say that
    you did.
